approach: Add a reading check `check_reader_question(reading: &Reading) -> Result<()>` in the new `crates/athena-core/src/reading/questions.rs`. It is declared in `reading.rs` (`mod questions; pub use questions::*;`) and run as the first `step!(check_reader_question(reading));` line of `refusing_check` in `reading/checks.rs`. That is where every reading-text rule runs: `read_for` reaches it through `check_reading_acceptance` (reading.rs:680) right after `build_reading`, so it covers the production path. `check_reading_text` (replay, `athena check-reading`, steward queue) and the refusal corpus reach it the same way. A reading with no question passes. A question is accepted only when it (1) begins `User:` (same normalisation as `admission::has_addressee`; `Host:` is not accepted, because the reader's question goes to the customer), (2) does not say the code answers it (reuse `says_code_answers`), (3) holds at least two distinct, non-empty alternatives labelled `(a)`, `(b)` or `(1)`, `(2)`, and (4) ends with `Default: (x)` where `(x)` is one of those labels. If not, the check bails with one message that lists every gap, the question, and the repair: settle it from the repository or defaults and leave `question` null, or rewrite it as `User:` + the decision + labelled alternatives + `Default: (x)`, with an example. `admission.rs` only widens visibility (`pub(crate)`) of `has_addressee` and `says_code_answers` and adds a small `pub(crate)` helper that tests for the `User:` prefix by the same normalisation. Planner open-questions behavior is unchanged. Unit tests, corpus cases (15 new input forms), the existing question tests (updated to the new format), a CHANGELOG entry and a design-doc paragraph complete it. A malformed first question costs one extra reader call, because `read_for` re-reads once with the refusal as a correction (reading.rs:489-514); the prompts stay untouched.

decisions.choice: Run the rule as a `step!` in `refusing_check` (checks.rs:518-547), first in the list, not as a bail inside `build_reading`.
decisions.reason: All reading-text rules live there. `no_check_bypasses_refusing_check` and `every_acceptance_check_has_a_refusing_corpus_case` (refusal_corpus.rs:2730, 2963) enforce it. `check_reading_text` (replay.rs:54; used by steward.rs:421 and `athena check-reading`) goes only through `refusing_check`, so a check in `build_reading` would be invisible to the replay that holds over-refusing jobs. `read_for` runs `build_reading` then `check_reading_acceptance` back to back (reading.rs:659-689), so the production path is the same. First place: the other checks skip a reading with a question or do not care, so the cheap question fix comes before other repairs and saves a reader round.

rejected.option: Call the rule from inside `build_reading` (the wording of criterion 1)
rejected.why: It would skip `check_reading_text`, the replay and the corpus mechanism, and the corpus test would flag a check outside `refusing_check`. `build_reading` is still on the path, since it builds the reading the step checks.
A reading with a bad question and another defect would be refused for the other defect first, costing an extra reader round.

decisions.choice: Require `User:` only; `Host:` is refused for the reader's question. Reuse `has_addressee` normalisation through a `pub(crate)` helper in admission.rs.
decisions.reason: Criterion 1 says a question that does not begin with `User:` is refused. The reader's question is shown to the customer (display.rs:392) and answered with `athena correct` (reading.rs:1202), so a host fact is not his decision. Sharing the normalisation (leading whitespace, `*`, `_`, backticks, case; `Username:` does not match) keeps one definition.

rejected.option: Accept `User:` or `Host:` as the planner does
rejected.why: Contradicts criterion 1, and a host fact is for the repository or defaults, not the customer.

rejected.option: Copy the prefix code into reading/questions.rs
rejected.why: Two definitions can drift; the brief asks for reuse.

decisions.choice: Detect alternatives by explicit labels `(a)`/`(b)` (or `(1)`/`(2)`), at least 2 distinct labels with non-empty, distinct text, and a default as `Default:` followed by one of those labels. The error shows the exact form.
decisions.reason: The check is deterministic and the finding can state the exact form the reader must write. Labels avoid guessing whether 'X or Y' is a real choice. The example in criterion 2 uses this form.

rejected.option: Count the word 'or' or question marks
rejected.why: A crude heuristic: 'hello or hi' passes with no default named, and 'is this ok or not' counts as two alternatives.

rejected.option: Accept `a)`, `1.` or prose 'either X or Y' as well
rejected.why: More forms mean more false accepts and a longer parser. The finding names the single accepted form, so a retry succeeds; a corpus case pins the unlabelled-'or' form as refused.

decisions.choice: Do not touch prompt files or the `question` schema description (outputs.rs:28); the refusal message carries the format.
decisions.reason: Out of scope: reader headroom is 71 tokens (system-facts budget reader 1929 of 2000). The refusal is fed back to the reader once (reading.rs:489-514).

rejected.option: Add the format to the reader frame
rejected.why: Out of scope; risks the 2000-token budget test `system_facts_budgets_match_computed`.

risks.risk: The reader does not know the required form before its first question, so every first question is refused once and `read_for` re-reads with the refusal (one extra reader call, reading.rs:489-514).
risks.mitigation: The error text carries the form and an example. If the second reading still has a malformed question, the job stops with the existing refusal path. The open question offers a schema-description follow-up.

risks.risk: Label parsing is rigid: `a)`, `1.` lists or prose 'either X or Y' are refused as having no alternatives, and a `Default:` placed before the alternatives is refused.
risks.mitigation: Rigidity is deliberate (criterion 1 asks for a checkable form). Corpus cases pin the refused forms, and the refusal text names the one accepted form.

risks.risk: `says_code_answers` matches phrases such as 'in the code' inside a legitimate alternative, so a real decision is refused.
risks.mitigation: Same phrase list and limits as the planner rule (admission.rs:559); the repair text says to rewrite the alternative. A corpus case pins one phrase.

risks.risk: Stored readings with free-form questions made before this change are refused by `check_reading_text`, so the steward leaves such a proposed job out of the drain until `athena go` (steward.rs:399).
risks.mitigation: This is the existing handling of a reading that fails a check and a re-read from `athena go` fixes it. The 3% declared share is an estimate, not measured; the replay at verification measures the real share.

risks.risk: The step goes in checks.rs, which the brief's deliverable list omits, so Athena may report it as a minor scope finding.
risks.mitigation: Reason recorded in decisions: `refusing_check` is defined in checks.rs and the corpus rule forbids any other call site.
